note: Wall-clock budgets for tests/e2e/perf.spec.ts (npm run test:perf). Human-set ceilings, not measurements — raise one only when you have decided the new cost is worth it, and say why in the commit. `measured` is refreshed by STEM_PERF_UPDATE=1 and is context only; nothing asserts on it.

plain.prompt: Reply with exactly the single word PONG in uppercase and nothing else.

web-search.prompt: Search the web and tell me in one sentence what the current stable version of Node.js is.

web-search-multi.note: The regression's exact shape — four queries in ONE web_search call. Serially that was ~13-17s per query; concurrently it is roughly one query's worth of wall clock. The prompt pins the tool usage on purpose: an open-ended research question measures the model's appetite for fetch_content (a dozen sequential page fetches, minutes of variance), not this code path.
web-search-multi.prompt: Call web_search exactly once, with these four queries: "Node.js current LTS version", "Python latest stable release", "Go latest stable release", "Rust latest stable release". Then answer in one short sentence from those results only. Do not fetch any pages and do not search again.

measured.headlessSplit: A/B across the Phase 1 headless split (2026-08-06), n=3 medians, same machine, back to back: the whole suite was run at 49fd444 (pre-split, one process, a direct callback from the backend to the window) and again on phase1/headless-split (the SSE hop in front of the render loop). plain: total 2003 -> 2110ms, ttft 1609 -> 1901ms, answer 127 -> 151ms. web-search: total 29723 -> 36474ms, tool 24389 -> 29516ms. web-search-multi: total 32880 -> 27189ms, tool 30109 -> 25152ms — FASTER after the split. The suite failed on BOTH sides (pre-split on web-search-multi.toolMs, post-split on web-search.totalMs and web-search-multi.toolMs), on the toolMs-dominated cases, which is the Exa-429 bimodality the note below describes and is time spent inside pi's search backends with none of Stem's transport on it. `plain`, the only case with no network tool in it, passes on both sides with room to spare. The transport's own cost is measured deterministically instead, in tests/e2e/stream-throughput.spec.ts: ~0.01ms per delta, embedded and external alike. Budgets deliberately NOT changed on the strength of any of this.
measured.note: Reference points from turn_timings on the author's machine, medians over web-search turns. Native provider-side search (<=2026-07-28): total 39.6s, tool 13.2s avg. Sequential pi-web-access (2026-07-29..08-02, the regression): total 99.8s, tool 127.1s avg. Then, on this harness: concurrent queries, total 15.4s / tool 12.4s; gpt-5.4-mini backing the OpenAI backend, 13.9s / 11.0s; auto reordered so an index lookup beats an inference, the numbers below. READ THOSE AS BIMODAL, not as a median with noise: a web_search that Exa answers costs 0.35-1.4s, and one where Exa returns HTTP 429 ('You've hit Exa's free MCP rate limit') falls through the chain to the OpenAI backend and costs 4-11s. Same run, both modes: 8276ms / 349ms / 8183ms. The mix depends on how much of the free tier is left, so the medians here drift with nothing in this repo changing. Configure an exaApiKey (or any keyed backend) in Settings and the 429 mode disappears.
